<p  align="center"><a name="os_001"></a><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>PART I</b></font></p>
<table align="center"  border="0" style="border-collapse:collapse" cellspacing="0"  cellpadding="0"  width="100%">

 <tr>
  <td width="10%" valign="top">
  <p>
<a name="os_002"></a><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>ITEM 1.</b></font></p>  </td>
  <td width="90%" valign="top">
  <p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>BUSINESS</b></font></p>  </td>
 </tr>
</table>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The disclosures set forth in this item are qualified by Item 1A. Risk Factors and the section captions &#147;General&#148; in Item 7. Management&#146;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations of this report and other cautionary statements set forth elsewhere in this report.</font></p>
<p><a name="os_003"></a>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>General</b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Oregon Steel Mills, Inc. (&#147;Company&#148; or &#147;Registrant&#148;) was founded in 1926 by William G. Gilmore and was incorporated in California in 1928. The Company reincorporated in Delaware in 1974. The Company changed its name in December 1987 from Gilmore Steel Corporation to Oregon Steel Mills, Inc.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;During 2005, the Company and its subsidiaries operated two steel mills and eight finishing facilities in the western United States and Canada. The Company manufactures and markets one of the broadest lines of specialty and commodity steel products of any domestic steel mill company.&#160; The Company emphasizes the cost efficient production of higher margin specialty steel products targeted at a diverse customer base located primarily west of the Mississippi River and in western Canada.&#160; The Company&#146;s manufacturing flexibility allows it to actively manage its product mix in response to changes in customer demand and individual product cycles.&#160; The Company is organized into two business units known as the Oregon Steel Division and Rocky Mountain Steel Mills (&#147;RMSM&#148;) Division.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Oregon Steel Division is centered on the Company&#146;s Portland, Oregon steel mill (&#147;Portland Mill&#148;), which has a Steckel combination mill that produces discrete steel plate and coiled plate for the division&#146;s steel plate heat-treating, structural tubing, and large diameter line pipe and electric resistance welded (&#147;ERW&#148;) pipe finishing facilities. The Oregon Steel Division produces large diameter line pipe and ERW line pipe and casing at its pipe mill in Camrose, Alberta, Canada (&#147;Camrose Pipe Mill&#148;).&#160; On March 30, 2005, the Company purchased the remaining 40% interest in the Camrose Pipe Mill, and now owns 100% of that facility.&#160; The Oregon Steel Division operates a temper mill and cut-to-length facility at its 60% owned Oregon Feralloy Partners (&#147;OFP&#148;) joint venture facility.&#160; In October 2003, the Oregon Steel Division began production
of structural tubing at its Columbia Structural Tubing (&#147;CST&#148;) facility. A large diameter pipe mill in Napa, California (&#147;Napa Mill&#148;) is also included in the Oregon Steel Division.&#160; This asset has not been used in the Company&#146;s operations subsequent to the Company&#146;s decision to permanently close the mill in 2004 and the real estate on which the Napa Mill equipment is located was sold in December of 2005.&#160; The Company is also in the process of constructing its spiral weld double submerged arc weld (&#147;DSAW&#148;) pipe making facility (&#147;Spiral Weld Mill&#148;) on the Portland Mill property.&#160; The construction of the Spiral Weld Mill is expected to be completed in July of 2006.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The RMSM Division consists of steelmaking and finishing facilities of CF&amp;I Steel, L.P. (&#147;CF&amp;I&#148;) (dba Rocky Mountain Steel Mills) located in Pueblo, Colorado (&#147;Pueblo Mill&#148;).&#160; The Company owns 90% of New CF&amp;I, Inc. (&#147;New CF&amp;I&#148;), which owns a 95.2% general partnership interest in CF&amp;I.&#160; In addition, the Company owns directly a 4.3% limited partnership interest in CF&amp;I.&#160; The Pueblo Mill is a steel minimill which supplies steel for the RMSM Division&#146;s rail, rod and bar, and seamless tubular finishing mills.&#160; The Pueblo Mill operates the only rail facility west of the Mississippi River, and is one of only two established rail manufacturers in North America.&#160; The RMSM Division also includes the Colorado and Wyoming Railroad Company, a wholly owned subsidiary of New CF&amp;I, which operates a short line railroad principally
servicing the Pueblo Mill.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b><i>Oregon Steel Division</i></b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Portland Mill</i>.&#160; The Portland Mill is the only hot-rolled steel plate minimill and steel plate production facility in the eleven western states.&#160; The Portland Mill melt shop has the capability to produce slab thicknesses of 6&#148;, 7&#148;, 8&#148; or 9&#148;.&#160; In May 2003, the Company shut down its Portland Mill melt shop and is currently producing its finished product from purchased steel slab.&#160; The Company continues to maintain the melt shop in operating condition.&#160; Purchased steel slabs are rolled in the Steckel combination mill (&#147;Combination Mill&#148;) located at the Portland Mill. The Combination Mill includes a 4-high rolling mill with coiling furnaces, a vertical edger, a down coiler, on-line accelerated cooling, hot leveling and shearing equipment, extended roll lines, and a fully automated hydraulic gauge control system. The Combination Mill gives the
Company the ability to produce steel plate in commercially preferred dimensions and sizes, increases its manufacturing flexibility and supplies substantially all the Company&#146;s plate requirements for large diameter line pipe manufactured at the Camrose Pipe Mill, as well as coiled plate for applications such as the smaller diameter ERW pipe manufactured at the Camrose Pipe Mill, structural tubing manufactured at CST and line pipe that will be manufactured at the Spiral Weld Mill.&#160; With the Combination Mill, the Company is positioned to produce all grades of discrete steel plate and coiled plate for substantially all of the Company&#146;s commodity and specialty markets, including heat-treated applications. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><i>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Napa Mill.</i>&#160; The Company decided to permanently close the Napa Mill in December 2004.&#160; In December 2005, the Company sold the related real estate and recorded an impairment charge for all related assets not transferred to other operating units.&#160; The Napa Mill was able to produce large diameter steel line pipe of a quality suitable for use in high pressure oil and gas transmission pipelines. The Napa Mill formerly produced pipe with an outside diameter ranging from 16&#148; to 42&#148;, with wall thicknesses of up to 1-1/16&#148; and in lengths of up to 80 feet, and could process two different sizes of pipe simultaneously in its two finishing sections.&#160; </font></p>

<p  align="center"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">1</font></p>

<div style="page-break-before:always"></div>
<PAGE>
<br>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Spiral Weld Mill.&#160; </i>In July 2004, the Company announced that its Board of Directors approved the construction of a spiral weld double submerged arc weld (&#147;DSAW&#148;) pipe making facility at its Portland Mill. The project consists of two pipe mills with an annual capacity of approximately 170,000 tons, depending on product mix, capable of producing API certified large diameter line pipe from 20 inches to 60 inches in diameter, in wall thickness of 1/4 inch to 1 inch, and in lengths of up to 80 feet. The construction of the Spiral Weld Mill is expected to be completed in July of 2006.&#160; </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Camrose Pipe Mill</i>.&#160; The Company acquired a 60% interest in the Camrose Pipe Mill in June 1992 from Stelco, Inc. (&#147;Stelco&#148;), a large Canadian steel producer.&#160; In March 2005, the Company acquired the remaining 40% interest and now owns 100% of the mill.&#160; The Camrose Pipe Mill has two pipe manufacturing mills, a large diameter line pipe mill similar to the Napa Mill and an ERW pipe mill which produces line pipe and casing used by the oil and gas industry. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Columbia Structural Tubing</i>.&#160; In October 2003, the Company leased (with an option to buy) the equipment of the former LTV Structural Tubing Facility.&#160; The leased equipment consists of a slitting line, a structural tubing mill, and a proprietary in-line coating system. The CST facility is located one mile from the Portland Mill and produces rectangular hollow steel sections (&#147;HSS&#148;) in sizes ranging from 2 &#189;&#148; to 10&#148;.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Oregon Feralloy Partners</i>. In June 1999, a wholly owned subsidiary of the Company and Feralloy Oregon Corporation formed OFP to construct a temper mill and a cut-to-length (&#147;CTL&#148;) facility to process CTL plate from steel coil produced at the Company&#146;s Portland Mill.&#160; The facility commenced operations in May 2001.&#160; The Company has a 60% profit/loss interest and Feralloy Oregon Corporation, the managing partner, has a 40% profit/loss interest in OFP. </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>RMSM Division</b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Shortly after the
acquisition of the Pueblo Mill in 1993, the Company began a series of major
capital improvements designed to increase yields, improve productivity and
quality, and expand the Company&#146;s ability to offer specialty rail, rod and
bar products.&#160; The primary components of the Pueblo Mill and the related
capital improvements, as appropriate, are outlined below.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Steelmaking</i>.&#160; The Company installed a ladle refining furnace and a vacuum degassing facility and upgraded both continuous casters with more efficient continuous casting methods that allow the Company to cast directly into bloom.&#160; In November 2005, the Company completed the conversion of its two existing furnaces to a new single AAa compliant furnace.&#160; </font></p>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Rod and Bar Mill.</i> At the time of its acquisition, the rod and bar mills at the Pueblo Mill were relatively old and located in separate facilities, which resulted in significant inefficiencies as the Company shifted production between them in response to market conditions.&#160; In 1995, the Company commenced operation of a new combination rod and bar mill with a new reheat furnace and a high speed rod train, capable of producing commodity and specialty grades of rod and bar products.&#160; These improvements have enabled the Company to produce a wider range of high margin specialty products, such as high-carbon rod, merchant bar and other specialty bar products, and larger rod coil sizes, which the Company believes are preferred by many of its customers. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><i>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Rail Manufacturing.</i>&#160; At the time of the Company&#146;s acquisition of the Pueblo Mill, rail was produced by ingot casting using energy-intensive processes with significant yield losses as the ingots were reheated, reduced to blooms and then rolled into rail. Continuous casting has increased rail yields and decreased rail manufacturing costs.&#160; In 1996, the Company invested in the Pueblo Mill&#146;s rail making capacity by entering into an agreement with Nippon for the license of its proprietary technology to produce deep head hardening (&#147;DHH&#148;) rail, and acquired the production equipment necessary to produce the specialty rail.&#160; DHH rail is considered by the rail industry to be longer lasting and of higher quality than rail produced using conventional methods and, accordingly, the DHH rail usually has a corresponding higher average selling price.&#160; The Company believes it
is able to meet the needs of a broad array of rail customers with both traditional and DHH rail.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><i>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Seamless Pipe.</i>&#160; The seamless pipe mill at the Pueblo Mill produces seamless casing, coupling stock and standard and line pipe. Seamless pipe casing is used as a structural retainer for the walls of oil or gas wells.&#160; Standard and line pipes are used to transport liquids and gasses both above and underground.&#160; The Company&#146;s seamless pipe mill is equipped to produce the most widely used sizes of seamless pipe (5&#148; outside diameter through 10-3/4&#148; outside diameter) in all standard lengths.&#160; The Company&#146;s production capability includes carbon and heat-treated tubular products.&#160; The Company has also sold semi-finished seamless pipe (referred to as green tubes) for processing and finishing by others. Operations at the seamless pipe mill were suspended from November 2003 until December 2005.&#160; In September 2005, the Company announced the reopening of the
seamless mill, with shipments beginning in January 2006.</font></p>

<p  align="center"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">2</font></p>

<p><a name="os_004"></a>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Products</b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b><i>Overview</i></b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company manufactures and markets one of the broadest lines of specialty and commodity steel products of any domestic minimill company.&#160; Through acquisitions and capital improvements, the Company has expanded its range of finished products from two in 1991, discrete plate and large diameter line pipe, to nine currently by adding ERW pipe, rail, rod, bar, seamless pipe, coiled plate and structural tubing.&#160; It has also expanded its primary selling region from the western United States to national and international markets.&#160; (See Note 3 to the Company&#146;s Consolidated Financial Statements, <i>&#147;Geographic Information.&#148;</i>) </font></p>
<p>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b><i>Oregon Steel Division</i></b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Steel Plate and Coiled Plate.</i>&#160; The Company&#146;s specialty grade and commodity steel plate and coiled plate are produced at the Portland Mill on the Combination Mill.&#160; The Combination Mill produces discrete steel plate in widths from 48&#148; to 136&#148; and in thicknesses from 3/16&#148; to 8&#148;.&#160; Coiled plate can be produced in widths of 48&#148; to 120&#148; and in thicknesses that range from 0.09&#148; to 0.75&#148;.&#160; The majority of steel plate is commonly produced and consumed in standard widths and lengths, such as 96&#148; x 240&#148;. Specialty steel plate consists of hot-rolled carbon, high-strength-low-alloy, alloy and heat-treated steel plate.&#160; Specialty steel plate has superior strength and performance characteristics as compared to commodity steel plate and is typically made to order for customers seeking specific properties, such as improved
malleability, hardness or abrasion resistance, impact resistance or toughness, higher strength and the ability to be more easily machined and welded.&#160; Specialty steel plate is used to manufacture railroad cars, mobile equipment, bridges and buildings, pressure vessels, machinery components and large diameter line pipe.&#160; Commodity steel plate is used in a variety of applications such as the manufacture of storage tanks, machinery parts, ships and barges, and general load bearing structures.&#160; Coiled plate is the feeder stock for the manufacture of ERW pipe, structural tubing, spiral weld pipe and for conversion into cut-to-length plate.&#160; </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The heat-treating process of quenching and tempering improves the strength, toughness, and hardness of the steel.&#160; Quenched and tempered steel is used extensively in the mining industry, the manufacture of heavy transportation equipment, construction and logging equipment, and armored vehicles for the military.&#160; In late 2004, the Company replaced and installed a hot leveler at the heat-treat facility which flattens the steel plate following heat-treatment.&#160; This ensures that the steel plate will retain its desired shape after cooling, thus continuing the Company&#146;s ability to manufacture a superior hardened plate product.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Large Diameter Line Pipe.</i>&#160; The Company manufactures large diameter, double submerged arc-welded (&#147;DSAW&#148;) steel line pipe at its Camrose Pipe Mill and manufactured DSAW steel line pipe through July 2004 at the Napa Mill.&#160; Large diameter line pipe is manufactured to demanding specifications and is produced in sizes ranging from 16&#148; to 42&#148; in outside diameter and in lengths of up to 80 feet.&#160; The Company also offers customers several options, which include internal linings, external coatings, and double end pipe joining. The Company&#146;s large diameter pipe is used primarily in pressurized underground or underwater oil and gas transmission pipelines where high quality is absolutely necessary.&#160;&#160; </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>ERW Pipe.</i> The Company produces smaller diameter ERW line pipe and casing at the Camrose Pipe Mill.&#160; ERW pipe is produced in sizes ranging from approximately 4 &#189;&#148; to 16&#148; in diameter.&#160; The pipe is manufactured using coiled steel formed on a high frequency ERW mill.&#160; The principal customers for this product are oil and gas companies that use it for gathering lines to supply product to feed larger pipeline systems and for casing for oil and gas wells. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Structural Tubing.</i> The Company produces rectangular HSS in sizes ranging from 2 &#189;&#148; to 10&#148;.&#160; These products have a wide variety of uses, including construction applications, structural support, safety and ornamental tubing for buildings, bridges, and highways and are also used for an extensive range of applications in industrial, transportation, and agricultural equipment.</font></p>
<p  align="center">
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">4</font></p>

<div style="page-break-before:always"></div>
<PAGE>
<br>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b><i>RMSM Division</i></b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Rail.</i>&#160; The Company produces standard carbon and high-strength head-hardened rail at its Pueblo Mill.&#160; The Pueblo Mill is the sole manufacturer of rail west of the Mississippi River and one of only two established rail manufacturers in North America. Rails are manufactured in the six most popular rail weights (ranging from 115 lb/yard through 141 lb/yard), in 39 and 80-foot lengths.&#160; In-line head-hardened rail is produced through a proprietary technology, known as deep head-hardened or DHH technology, which is licensed from a third party.&#160; In 2005, the Company produced approximately 179,000 tons of head-hardened product using the DHH technology.&#160; The in-line DHH technology allows the Company to produce head-hardened product up to the capacity of the rail facility.&#160; Rail produced using the improved in-line technology is considered by many rail customers to be longer
lasting and of higher quality than rail produced with traditional off-line techniques.&#160; Since 2001, the Pueblo Mill has produced and marketed an improved head-hardened rail called High Carbon Pearlite.&#160; This rail metallurgy was designed for heavy application situations such as heavy tonnage curves.&#160; The primary customers for the Pueblo Mill&#146;s rail are the western railroads.&#160; The Company has also developed a presence in the Canadian and Mexican rail markets.&#160; Rail is also sold directly to rail contractors, transit districts, and short-line railroads. </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Rod and</i> <i>Bar Products.</i>&#160; The Company&#146;s rod and bar mill located at the Pueblo Mill is able to produce coils of up to 6,000 pounds.&#160; The steel quality and finishing capabilities allow the Company to manufacture rods up to 1&#148; in diameter, and to manufacture a variety of high-carbon rod products such as those used for spring wire, wire rope, and tire bead. The Company produces several sizes of coiled rebar in the most popular grades for the reinforcement of concrete products.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<i>Seamless Pipe.&#160;&#160; </i>The Company&#146;s seamless pipe mill at the Pueblo Mill can produce seamless casing and standard and line pipe.&#160; The primary use of these products is in the transmission and recovery of oil and natural gas resources, through either above ground or subterranean pipelines.&#160; The seamless mill can produce both carbon and heat-treated tubular products.&#160; The Company has also sold green tubes to other tubular mills for processing and finishing. </font></p>
<p><a name="os_005"></a>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Raw Materials and Semi-finished Slabs</b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><i>Oregon Steel Division </i></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Portland Mill relies on purchased semi-finished steel slabs for the production of plate and coiled plate.&#160; The steel slab market and pricing are subject to significant volatility and steel slabs may not be available at reasonable prices in the future.&#160; </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In May 2003, the Company shut down its Portland Mill melt shop. The determination to close the melt shop was based on the Company&#146;s ability to obtain steel slab through purchases from suppliers on the open market, and the high energy and raw material costs and the yield losses associated with the inefficient casting technology in use at the Portland Mill.&#160; The Company forecasts that future steel slab purchases for the Portland Mill will meet the production needs of the Portland Mill finishing operation for 2006 and into the foreseeable future. The Company continues to maintain the melt shop in operating condition.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><i>RMSM Division</i></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company&#146;s principal raw material for the Pueblo Mill is ferrous scrap metal derived from, among other sources, junked automobiles, railroad cars and railroad track materials and demolition scrap from obsolete structures, containers, and machines.&#160; In addition, direct-reduction iron, hot-briquetted iron and pig iron (collectively &#147;alternate metallics&#148;) can substitute for a limited portion of the scrap used in minimill steel production, although the sources and availability of alternate metallics are substantially more limited than those of scrap.&#160; The purchase prices for scrap and alternate metallics are subject to market forces largely beyond the control of the Company, and are impacted by demand from domestic and foreign steel producers, freight costs, speculation by scrap brokers, and other conditions.&#160; The cost of scrap and alternate metallics to the Company can vary
significantly, and the Company&#146;s product prices cannot in all cases be adjusted to fully recover the cost increases in scrap and alternate metallics prices. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The long-term demand for steel scrap and its importance to the domestic steel industry may increase as steelmakers continue to expand scrap-based electric arc furnace capacity; however, the Company believes that near-term supplies of steel scrap will continue to be available in sufficient quantities at competitive prices.&#160; In addition, while alternate metallics are not currently cost competitive with steel scrap, a sustained increase in the price of steel scrap could result in increased implementation of these alternative materials. </font></p>
<p><a name="os_006"></a>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Marketing and Customers</b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Steel products are sold by the Company principally through its own sales organizations, which have sales offices at various locations in the United States and Canada and, as appropriate, through foreign sales agents. In addition to selling to customers who consume steel products directly, the Company also sells to intermediaries such as steel service centers, distributors, processors and converters.&#160; No single customer or group of affiliated customers represented more than 10% of the Company&#146;s sales revenue in 2005, 2004 or 2003. </font></p>

<p  align="center"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">5</font></p>

<div style="page-break-before:always"></div>
<PAGE>
<br>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The sales force is organized both geographically and by product line.&#160; The Company has separate sales forces for plate and coiled plate, large diameter line pipe and ERW pipe, structural tubing, rod and bar, seamless pipe and rail products.&#160; Most of the Company&#146;s sales are initiated by contacts between sales representatives and customers.&#160; Accordingly, the Company does not incur substantial advertising or other promotional expenses for the sale of its products.&#160; Except for contracts entered into from time to time to supply rail and large diameter line pipe to significant projects, the Company does not have any significant ongoing contracts with customers, and orders placed with the Company generally are cancelable by the customer prior to production.&#160; </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company has a general policy permitting returns of purchased steel products only for product defects. The Company does not routinely offer extended payment terms to its customers.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Some of the Company&#146;s products are subject to seasonal trends.&#160; The Company&#146;s rail products are impacted by seasonal demand, as dictated by the major railroads&#146; procurement schedules.&#160; Demand for oil country tubular goods (&#147;OCTG&#148;), which include both seamless pipe and ERW pipe, can be subject to seasonal factors, particularly for sales to Canadian customers.&#160; Overall demand for OCTG is subject to significant fluctuations due to the volatility of oil and gas prices and North American drilling activity as well as other factors including competition from imports.&#160; </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b><i>Oregon Steel Division</i></b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><i>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Specialty Steel Plate</i>.&#160; Customers for specialty steel are located throughout the United States, but the Company is most competitive west of the Mississippi River, where transportation costs are less of a factor. Typical customers include steel service centers and equipment manufacturers.&#160; </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Commodity Steel Plate.</i>&#160; Most of the customers for the Company&#146;s commodity steel plate are located in the western United States, primarily in the Pacific Northwest.&#160; In addition to being used internally as feeder stock in the Company&#146;s manufacture of large diameter line pipe, steel plate is typically sold to steel service centers, fabricators, and equipment manufacturers.&#160; Service centers typically resell to other users with or without additional processing such as cutting to a specific shape.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Large Diameter Steel Line Pipe.</i>&#160; Large diameter line pipe is marketed on a global basis, and sales generally consist of a small number of large orders from natural gas pipeline companies, public utilities, and oil and gas producing companies.&#160; Sales of large diameter line pipe generally involve the Company responding to requests to submit bids.&#160;&#160; </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>ERW Pipe.</i>&#160; The principal customers for ERW line pipe and casing produced at the Camrose Pipe Mill are in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia, where most of Canada&#146;s natural gas and oil reserves are located.&#160; The Company believes its proximity to these gas fields gives the Company a competitive advantage. Demand for ERW pipe produced at the Camrose Pipe Mill is largely dependent on the level of exploration and drilling activity in the gas fields of western Canada. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><i>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Structural Tubing.</i>&#160; The majority of customers for the Company&#146;s structural tubing products are steel service centers located in Oregon and Washington.&#160; The Company has also been successful in expanding into other regions including Alaska, British Columbia, Montana, and Idaho.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b><i>RMSM Division</i></b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Rail.</i>&#160;
The primary customers for the Pueblo Mill&#146;s rail are the western railroads.

The Company has also developed a presence in the Canadian and Mexican rail
markets.&#160; Rail is also sold directly to rail distributors, transit
districts and short-line railroads.&#160; The Company believes its proximity to
the North American rail markets benefits its marketing efforts.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Rod and Bar Products.</i>&#160; The Company sells its bar products, primarily reinforcing bar, to fabricators and distributors.&#160; The majority of these customers are located in the United States, west of the Mississippi River.&#160;&#160; The Company&#146;s wire rod products are sold primarily to wire drawers ranging in location from the Midwest to the West Coast.&#160; The demand for wire rod is dependent upon a wide variety of markets, including agricultural, construction, capital equipment, and the durable goods segments.&#160; The Company entered the high carbon rod market during 1995 as a direct result of the investment in the new rolling facility.&#160; Since that time, the Company&#146;s participation in the higher margin, high carbon rod market has steadily increased, to the point where it now represents over two-thirds of its total rod product shipments.&#160; Typical end uses of high
carbon rod include spring wire, wire rope and tire bead.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Seamless Pipe.</i>&#160; The Company&#146;s seamless pipe will be sold directly to one customer who in turn will thread the Company&#146;s plain end pipe.&#160; The customer will then sell the finished pipe to oil exploration and production companies within the OCTG industry.&#160; The market for the Company&#146;s seamless pipe is primarily domestic.&#160; The demand for this product is determined in large part by the number and drilling depths of the oil and gas drilling rigs working in the United States.</font></p>
<p  align="center">
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">6</font></p>

<div style="page-break-before:always"></div>
<PAGE>
<br>

<p><a name="os_007"></a>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Competition and Other Market Factors</b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The steel industry is cyclical in nature.&#160; High levels of steel imports, worldwide production over capacity and other factors have adversely affected the domestic steel industry in recent years.&#160; The Company is also subject to industry trends and conditions, such as the presence or absence of sustained economic growth and construction activity, currency exchange rates and other factors.&#160; The Company is particularly sensitive to trends in the oil and gas, construction, capital equipment, rail transportation, and durable goods segments, because these industries are significant markets for the Company&#146;s products. </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Competition within the steel industry is intense.&#160; The Company competes primarily on the basis of product quality, price, and responsiveness to customer needs.&#160; Many of the Company&#146;s competitors are larger and have substantially greater capital resources, more modern technology, and may have lower labor and raw material costs than the Company.&#160; Moreover, United States steel producers have historically faced significant competition from foreign producers.&#160; The highly competitive nature of the industry, combined with excess production capacity in some products can result in significant sales pricing pressure for certain of the Company&#146;s products. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b><i>Oregon Steel Division</i></b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Specialty Steel Plate.</i>&#160; The Company&#146;s principal domestic competitor in the specialty steel plate market is Mittal Steel (&#147;Mittal&#148;), the largest plate producer in North America with six plate mills located in the Midwest and East. Mittal&#146;s estimated plate-making capacity now exceeds 3 million tons, including the largest plate heat-treating tonnage capacity in North America.&#160; Mittal aggressively markets to major national accounts in fabrication and heavy-duty manufacturing as a single source supplier. IPSCO Inc. (&#147;IPSCO&#148;) has also announced their intention to begin operations in 2006 of a new continuous plate-heat treating plant with an annual capacity of approximately 170,000 tons. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Commodity Steel Plate.</i>&#160; The Company&#146;s principal domestic commodity plate competitor is IPSCO.&#160; IPSCO operates a 120&#148; wide Steckel mill in Iowa, with that mill operating to nearly the same specifications as the Portland Mill.&#160; IPSCO also operates a smaller 72&#148; wide Steckel mill in Saskatchewan, Canada, and a 120&#148; wide Steckel mill in Mobile, Alabama.&#160; IPSCO&#146;s rated plate and coiled plate capacity exceeds three million tons annually. IPSCO also operates cut-to-length lines (to convert coiled plate into flat sheets) in various market locations throughout North America.&#160; IPSCO competes primarily in the Midwest commodity plate market, in other selected target markets, and in the coiled plate market throughout the United States.&#160; Nucor Corporation operates a plate mill at Hertford, North Carolina with an operating capacity of one million tons per
year and a Steckel mill at Tuscaloosa, Alabama with an operating capacity of approximately six hundred thousand tons per year. </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Large Diameter Steel Line Pipe</i>.&#160; The Company&#146;s principal domestic competitors in the large diameter line pipe market are Berg Steel Pipe Corporation, located in Florida, and South Texas Steel, located in Texas.&#160; International competitors consist primarily of pipe producers from Japan, Europe, and Canada, with the principal Canadian competitor being IPSCO.&#160; Demand for the Company&#146;s pipe in recent years is primarily a function of new construction of oil and gas transportation pipelines and to a lesser extent maintenance and replacement of existing pipelines.&#160; Construction of new pipelines domestically depends to some degree on the level of oil and gas exploration and drilling activity.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>ERW Pipe. </i>&#160;The competition in the market for ERW line pipe and casing is based on availability, price, product quality, and responsiveness to customers.&#160; The need for this product has a direct correlation to the number of drilling rigs in the United States and Canada. Principal competitors in the ERW product in Western Canada are IPSCO and Prudential Steel Ltd. located in Calgary, Alberta, a wholly owned subsidiary of Maverick Tube Corporation. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><i>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Structural Tubing. </i>&#160;&#160;The Company&#146;s primary competitors in the structural tubing market are Maruichi America Corporation, and Vest Industries both located in the Los Angeles, California vicinity.&#160; Other competitors are located in the Midwest and Western United States as well as importers from Asia.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b><i>RMSM Division</i></b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Rail.</i>&#160; The majority of current rail requirements in the United States are replacement rails for existing rail lines.&#160; Imports have been a significant factor in the domestic rail market in recent years.&#160; The Company&#146;s capital expenditure program at the Pueblo Mill provided the rail production facilities with continuous cast steel capability and in-line head-hardening rail capabilities necessary to compete with other producers.&#160; Mittal is the only other qualified domestic rail producer at this time.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Rod and
Bar</i>.&#160; The competition in bar products includes a group of minimills
that have a geographical location close to the markets in or around the Rocky
Mountains.&#160; The Company&#146;s market for wire rod ranges from the Midwest
to the West Coast.&#160; Domestic rod competitors include Gerdau Ameristeel
Corporation, Cascade Steel Rolling Mills, and Keystone Steel and Wire for
commodity grades and Mittal, Ivaco Rolling Mills, and Gerdau Ameristeel
Corporation for high carbon rod products. </font></p>
<p  align="center">
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">7</font></p>

<div style="page-break-before:always"></div>
<PAGE>
<br>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Seamless Pipe</i>.&#160; The Company&#146;s primary competitors in seamless pipe include a number of domestic and foreign manufacturers.&#160; The Company has the flexibility to produce relatively small volumes of specified products on short notice in response to customer requirements. Principal domestic competitors include U.S. Steel Corporation and V&amp;M Star for seamless product.&#160; Lone Star Steel competes with its welded ERW pipe in lieu of seamless, which is acceptable for some applications.</font></p>
<p><a name="os_008"></a>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Environmental Matters</b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company is subject to extensive environmental laws and regulations by foreign, federal, state and local governmental agencies.&#160; Environmental concerns include, among other things, wastewater, stormwater, air emissions, toxic use reduction and hazardous materials disposal.&#160; Like other similar steel mills in the industry, the Pueblo Mill generates, and the Portland Mill has, in the past, generated hazardous waste from the melting operation of the electric arc furnaces, primarily dust containing heavy metals.&#160; This dust, which constitutes the largest waste stream generated at these facilities, must be managed in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Clean Air Act Amendments (&#147;CAA&#148;) of 1990 imposed responsibilities on many industrial sources of air emissions, including the Company&#146;s plants.&#160; In addition, the monitoring and reporting requirements of the law subject all companies with significant air emissions to increased regulatory scrutiny.&#160; The Company submitted applications in 1995 to the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (&#147;DEQ&#148;) and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (&#147;CDPHE&#148;) for permits under Title V of the CAA for the Portland and Pueblo mills, respectively.&#160; A Title V permit was issued for the Portland Mill and related operations in December 2000 and modified in April 2002 and again in January 2006 in relation to the construction in progress of the Spiral Weld Mill.&#160; See Note 16 to the Company&#146;s Consolidated Financial Statements,
<i>&#147;Contingencies,&#148;</i> for a description of CAA compliance issues relating to the Pueblo Mill.&#160; The Company does not know the ultimate cost of compliance with the CAA, which will depend on a number of site-specific factors.&#160; Regardless of the outcome of the environmental matters discussed in Note 16 to the Company&#146;s Consolidated Financial Statements, the Company anticipates that it will be required to incur additional expenses and make additional capital expenditures as a result of the CAA and future laws regulating air emissions.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company&#146;s future expenditures for installation of, and improvements to, environmental control facilities, remediation of environmental conditions, penalties for violations of environmental laws, and other similar matters are difficult to predict accurately.&#160; It is likely that the Company will be subject to increasingly stringent environmental standards, including those relating to air emissions, waste water and stormwater discharge and hazardous materials use, storage, handling and disposal.&#160; It is also likely that the Company will be required to make potentially significant expenditures relating to environmental matters, including environmental remediation, on an ongoing basis.&#160; Although the Company has established reserves for certain environmental matters, including those described in Note 16 to the Company&#146;s Consolidated Financial Statements, additional measures may be
required by environmental authorities or as a result of additional environmental hazards, identified by such authorities, the Company or others, each necessitating further expenditure.&#160; Accordingly, the costs of environmental matters may exceed the amounts reserved.&#160; Expenditures of the nature described in Note 16 to the Company&#146;s Consolidated Financial Statements or liabilities resulting from hazardous substances located on the Company&#146;s currently or previously owned properties or used or generated in the conduct of the Company&#146;s business, or resulting from circumstances, actions, proceedings or claims relating to environmental matters, may have a material adverse effect on the Company&#146;s consolidated financial condition, results of operations, or cash flows.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><i>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</i>See Note 16 to the Company&#146;s Consolidated Financial Statements, <i>&#147;Contingencies,&#148;</i> for a discussion of specific environmental matters.</font></p>
<p><a name="os_009"></a>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Employees</b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As of December 31, 2005, the Company had approximately 1,680 full-time active employees. The Oregon Steel Division employs approximately 800 employees including corporate employees.&#160; None of the employees of the Portland Mill, CST, and the corporate headquarters are represented by a union. Approximately 250 employees at the Camrose Pipe Mill are members of the Canadian Autoworkers Union (&#147;CAW&#148;) and are working under the terms of a collective bargaining agreement that expired in January 2006.&#160; The Company and the CAW are currently negotiating the terms of a new bargaining agreement.&#160; The RMSM Division employs approximately 880 employees, approximately 670 of which work under collective bargaining agreements with several unions, including the United Steelworkers of America (&#147;Union&#148;).&#160; The Company and the Union have entered into new labor agreements in September 2004
that expire in 2009. See &#147;<i>Item 7. &#150; Management&#146;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations &#150; Labor Dispute Settlement Charges&#148;. </i>The Colorado and Wyoming Railway Company labor agreements expire in March 2006 and May 2007. </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company has domestic profit participation plans under which it distributes quarterly to eligible employees 5% of its operating income after adjustments for certain non-operating items.&#160; The Company also distributes quarterly to eligible Camrose Pipe Mill employees profit participation based on a sliding scale of annualized profits.&#160; Under both plans, each eligible employee receives a share of the distribution based upon the employee&#146;s base compensation in relation to the total base compensation of all eligible employees of the operating unit.&#160; In addition, the Company offers an annual incentive plan to approximately 60 senior managers and officers based upon certain financial and operational performance criteria established for that year.&#160; The Company may modify, amend or terminate the plans, at any time, subject to the terms of various labor agreements.</font></p>

  <p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>RISK FACTORS</b></font></p>  </td>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition to the other information contained in this Form 10-K, the following risk factors should be considered carefully in evaluating the Company&#146;s business.&#160; The Company&#146;s business, financial condition or results of operations could be materially adversely affected by any of these risks.&#160; Please note that additional risks not presently known to the Company or that the Company currently deems immaterial may also impair its business and operations.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>The steel industry is cyclical, and has experienced periods of weak demand for products, excess capacity and low prices.&#160; If those conditions return the Company could be required to reduce prices for its products and profitability could be adversely impacted. </b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Downturns in the industry have caused steel companies to file for bankruptcy, including some that are substantially larger than the Company. High fixed costs motivate steel producers to maintain high output levels even in the face of falling prices, thereby increasing further downward pressures on selling prices.&#160; Increased demand for steel products in Asia, a weak United States dollar, high ocean freight cost, improving conditions in the manufacturing economy, and reduced United States steel production capacity have significantly reduced worldwide oversupply and excess capacity. As a result, the Company, and the domestic steel industry in general, have recently seen significant increases in the selling prices of steel products which peaked in the fourth quarter of 2004.&#160; However, if the domestic steel industry again experiences reduced demand, overcapacity and reduced selling prices for steel
products, the Company&#146;s ability to realize its target profit margins will be impaired and its results of operations could be materially and adversely affected.&#160;&#160; </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Increased levels of imports could have an adverse effect on the Company&#146;s business. </b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Foreign
competition historically has adversely affected product prices in the United
States and the tonnage sold by domestic steel producers. Fluctuations in the
value of the United States dollar against several other currencies substantially
affect the intensity of foreign competition. Foreign governments control or
subsidize many foreign steel producers. Decisions by these producers concerning
production and exports may be influenced, in part, by political and social
policy considerations as well as by prevailing market conditions and profit
opportunities. Economic and currency dislocations in foreign markets may
encourage importers to target the United States with excess capacity at
aggressive prices. Moreover, existing trade laws and regulations may be
inadequate to prevent unfair trade practices concerning these imports that could
pose increasing problems for the Company and the rest of the domestic steel
industry. Any such competition may have an adverse effect on the Company&#146;s production,
sales, operating margins, and profitability. </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>The inputs used in production are subject to price fluctuations that could increase the costs of production and adversely affect the Company&#146;s profitability. </b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The purchase prices for scrap and alternate metallics used at the Company&#146;s RMSM Division are affected by cyclical, seasonal, and other market factors. Prices also fluctuate on the basis of factors affecting supply, such as demand from domestic and foreign steel producers, periodic shortages, freight costs, speculation by brokers, export markets, and other conditions. Most of these factors are beyond the Company&#146;s control. The cost of scrap and alternate metallics can vary significantly, and finished product prices often cannot be adjusted, especially in the short-term, to recover those increased costs.&#160; </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition
to scrap and alternate metallics, the Company purchases steel slabs on the open
market for its Portland Mill.&#160; Purchased slabs are expected to represent
100% of the production needs for plate and coiled plate in the foreseeable
future. Even though the Company has established procurement relationships with
certain vendors, it does not have any long-term steel slab supply agreements.
The steel slab market and pricing are subject to significant volatility, and
steel slabs may not be available at reasonable prices in the future or at the
times and in the quantities needed to satisfy the Company&#146;s customers. In addition, any
significant increases in the price of steel slabs that cannot be passed along
through higher priced finished products to the Company&#146;s customers could
have a materially adverse affect on the Company&#146;s gross margins and
operating results.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, an increase in specific utility rates, such as natural gas or electricity, or other service costs could have an adverse effect on the Company&#146;s margins if those costs cannot be passed along to the Company&#146;s customers.</font></p>
<p  align="center">
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">9</font></p>

<div style="page-break-before:always"></div>
<PAGE>
<br>


<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Supply limitations or delays,
including those resulting from trade tariffs or quotas or port closures, would
constrain the Company&#146;s production and could materially and adversely
affect its sales and profitability. </b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company
purchases steel slabs from a number of foreign producers.&#160; Any interruption
or reduction in the supply of steel slabs may make it difficult or impossible to
satisfy customers&#146; delivery requirements, which could have a material
adverse effect on the Company&#146;s results of operations. Steel slabs are
purchased from a number of foreign producers. Most of the steel slabs purchased
are delivered by ship. Any disruption to port operations, including those caused
by a labor dispute or terrorism, could materially impact the supply or the cost
of steel slabs, which could have a material adverse effect on the Company&#146;s
production, sales levels, and profitability. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, the imposition of tariffs pursuant to trade laws and regulations can have an adverse impact on the Company&#146;s business by placing tariffs and tariff-rate quotas on the import of steel slabs and raising the prices of steel slabs used in production. Future impositions of tariffs or quotas could limit access to steel slabs at reasonable cost, or at all, and could consequently have a material adverse effect on the Company&#146;s production, sales levels, operating margins, and profitability. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>The Company services cyclical industries and generally does not have long-term contracts with its customers, and therefore any downturn in these industries could reduce revenue and profitability. </b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company sells products within cyclical industries, such as the rail transportation, construction, capital equipment, oil and gas, and durable goods segments. The demand for these products can change as a result of economic conditions, energy prices or other factors beyond the Company&#146;s control. As a result of the volatile industries, the Company may have difficulty increasing or maintaining sales and profitability if it is not able to divert product to customers in other industries during these periods of decline. </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company does not have significant ongoing contracts with customers, and orders taken are generally cancelable by the customer prior to production. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>The Company&#146;s substantial amount
of debt could materially and adversely affect its financial health in a number
of ways, including limiting its ability to obtain additional financing and
reducing its ability to use cash flow for purposes other than debt payments, and
prevent the Company from fulfilling its obligations under the outstanding debt.
</b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company&#146;s debt is secured by the Company&#146;s assets including the assets of its subsidiaries.&#160; The Company&#146;s debt could have the following adverse consequences:</font></p>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If the Company is unable to satisfy its debt obligations, it could result in all of the debt becoming immediately due and payable and could permit the lenders to foreclose on the assets securing the debt. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>The Company may not be able to generate sufficient cash flow to service its debt which could prevent the Company from fulfilling its obligations under its outstanding debt.&#160; </b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company may not be able to generate sufficient cash flow to service its debt, to repay its debt when due or to meet unanticipated capital needs. The Company plans to service interest payments on its debt with cash from operations. The Company&#146;s cash from operations, however, may not be sufficient to repay the principal amount on the outstanding debt when it becomes due. </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company&#146;s ability to generate
sufficient cash flow to satisfy its obligations will depend on its future
performance, which is subject to many economic, political, competitive,
regulatory, and other factors that are beyond the Company&#146;s control. In
addition, the Company faces potential costs and liabilities associated with
environmental compliance and remediation issues. If cash from operations is not
sufficient to satisfy the Company&#146;s obligations, it may need to seek
additional financing in the debt or equity markets, refinance the debt, sell
selected assets or reduce or delay planned activities and capital expenditures.
Any such financing, refinancing or sale of assets might not be available on
economically favorable terms, if at all. If the Company cannot meet its debt
service requirements an event of default would occur under the debt instruments.
This could result in all of the Company&#146;s debt becoming immediately due and
payable and could permit the Company&#146;s lenders to foreclose on its assets,
or the assets of its subsidiaries securing the debt. </font></p>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>The Company&#146;s pension plans are currently underfunded and are at risk of becoming more underfunded due to changes in interest rates or due to the performance of pension plan assets that are invested in capital markets.&#160; </b></font></p>
<p  align="center">
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">10</font></p>

<div style="page-break-before:always"></div>
<PAGE>
<br>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;All of the Company&#146;s pension plans are currently underfunded, and under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the Company is required to record a liability to reflect the total underfunded accumulated benefit obligation (ABO) on its balance sheets.&#160; The amount of underfunded ABO is dependent on changes in interest rates, investment performance (as compared to the long-term expected rate of return on plan assets, which is dependent on the investment strategy) and the level of Company contributions.&#160; Changes in any of these factors could cause a dramatic change in the amount of liability, as well as the total pension expense recorded in the Company&#146;s Consolidated Financial Statements.&#160; Factors that can affect the amount of cash funding requirements include future asset performance, the level of interest rates used to measure minimum funding levels, union negotiated changes and
future government regulation.&#160; Minimum funding requirements could have a materially adverse effect on the Company&#146;s cash flows.&#160; </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>The Company faces significant competition in its principal markets, and increased competition could reduce gross margins and net income. </b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The principal markets served are highly competitive. Steel manufacturers compete primarily on the basis of product quality, price, and responsiveness to customer needs. Many of the Company&#146;s competitors are larger and have substantial capital resources. Consolidation within the industry has increased the size of some of the competitors. Increased competition, especially combined with excess production capacity in some products, could force the Company to lower its prices, reducing gross margins and net income. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Unplanned repairs, equipment outages, and delays in capital expansion projects could interrupt production and reduce income or cash flow. </b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company&#146;s operations depend
upon critical pieces of equipment that are occasionally out of service for
routine scheduled maintenance, equipment failures, or due to unforeseen delays
in capital expansion. Any unplanned unavailability of critical equipment or
delays in capital expansion projects would interrupt the Company&#146;s production capabilities
and reduce sales and profitability. Although failures in significant equipment
are uncommon, there could be material shutdowns in the future. </font></p>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>The resolution of pending environmental actions and the costs of compliance with environmental orders and regulations may materially and adversely affect the Company&#146;s competitiveness and profitability. </b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company is subject to extensive foreign, federal, state, and local environmental laws and regulations concerning, among other things, wastewater, stormwater, air emissions, toxic use reduction and hazardous materials storage, handling, and disposal. Like other similar steel mills in the industry, the Pueblo Mill generates hazardous waste from the melting operation of its electric arc furnace, primarily dust containing heavy metals. Environmental standards are becoming increasingly stringent, including those relating to air emissions, waste water and stormwater discharge and hazardous materials use, storage, handling, and disposal, and the Company will likely be required to make additional expenditures, which could be significant, relating to environmental matters on an ongoing basis. Although reserves for environmental remediation have been established, the cost of remedial measures that might
eventually be required by environmental authorities may exceed those reserves. Furthermore, additional environmental claims which are in excess of the current reserves or not reserved for at all, might be asserted by environmental authorities or private parties. The Company&#146;s insurance policies surrounding the Portland Mill&#146;s environmental matters may not provide sufficient coverage for all remediation costs which are currently not known as they continue to be dependent on several ongoing investigations.&#160;&#160; The Company may also be subject to legal proceedings brought by private parties or governmental agencies with respect to environmental matters, which could have a material adverse effect on the Company&#146;s business.&#160;&#160; See Note 16 to the Company&#146;s Consolidated Financial Statements, <i>&#147;Contingencies,&#148;</i> for a description of the current environmental matters.</font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>A portion of the Company&#146;s workforce is unionized; any labor disruptions, work stoppages or significant negotiated wage increases could reduce sales or increase costs, and accordingly could have an adverse effect on the Company&#146;s business. </b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company&#146;s unionized employees consist primarily of hourly production workers. Most of the employees at the Pueblo Mill and the Camrose Pipe Mill belong to unions, and those mills negotiate collective bargaining agreements with these unions. Any failure to reach agreement on new labor agreements when required might result in a work stoppage that could, depending upon the operations affected and the length of the work stoppage, have a material adverse effect on the Company&#146;s operations.&#160; In addition, a contract may be renegotiated with significant increases in wages or other adverse economic terms, which would increase costs and reduce profitability. The Company and the CAW are currently negotiating the terms of a new bargaining agreement for the Camrose Pipe Mill employees.&#160; There has not been a work stoppage related to the expired agreement.&#160; See <i>&#147;Item 1. Business
&#150; Employees,&#148;</i> for further discussion of existing labor contracts.&#160; As part of the 2004 settlement with the Union, the Company does not get involved, directly or indirectly, in any matter that involves the unionization of employees at the Portland Mill or CST. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>The Company offers stock compensation to certain employees and non-employee directors which can vary based on the Company&#146;s operating performance, as well as market related factors which are outside the Company&#146;s control.&#160; In addition, a portion of the expense associated with the awards varies based on the price of the Company&#146;s common stock, which may fluctuate substantially.&#160; </b></font></p>
<p  align="center">
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">11</font></p>

<div style="page-break-before:always"></div>
<PAGE>
<br>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Part of the compensation offered
to certain executives, key employees, and non-employee directors is share-based
in its nature.&#160; The Company has granted, and in the future expects to
continue to grant, performance based awards under its 2005 Long-Term Incentive
Plan.&#160; The performance awards are based on the Company&#146;s performance against (1) the
total shareholder return as compared to a pre-determined peer group, and (2) the
three-year average earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and
amortization per ton shipped.&#160; One half of the total performance awards are
earned based on each category, and awards are paid 60% in cash and 40% in the
Company&#146;s common stock.&#160; Generally Accepted Accounting Principles
dictate that the accounting for these awards is based on fair value principles
beginning on January 1, 2006.&#160; The Company may be subject to variable
levels of expense related primarily to the cash settled portion of the awards
based on varying levels of performance, as well as for fluctuations in the
Company&#146;s stock price as a portion of these awards are &#147;marked to
market&#148; periodically over the three-year service period.&#160; </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The market price of the Company&#146;s common stock is likely to be highly volatile and may fluctuate substantially due to many factors including:</font></p>

Company&#146;s operating performance.&#160; </font></p>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>Senior management may be difficult to replace if they leave. </b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company&#146;s operations and prospects
depend in large part on the performance of the Company&#146;s senior management team, including
its chief executive officer and president, chief financial officer and the
other members of the senior management team. The loss of the services of one or
more of these members or the inability to attract, retain and maintain
additional or replacement senior management personnel could harm the
Company&#146;s business, financial condition, results of operations and future
prospects.&#160; The Company does not have key man insurance on any of its
executives.</font></p>

  <p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>PROPERTIES</b></font></p>  </td>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b><i>Oregon Steel Division</i></b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Portland Mill is located on approximately 143 acres owned by the Company in the Rivergate Industrial Park in Portland, Oregon, near the confluence of the Columbia and Willamette rivers. The operating facilities principally consist of a melt shop which includes an electric arc furnace, ladle metallurgy station, vacuum degasser, steel slab casting equipment and the Combination Mill, as well as an administrative office building.&#160; In May 2003, the Company shut down its Portland Mill melt shop but continues to maintain the melt shop in operating condition.&#160; The Company&#146;s heat-treating facilities are located nearby on a 5-acre site owned by the Company.&#160; In 2005, the Company began construction of a new spiral weld DSAW pipe mill.&#160; The Spiral Weld Mill is expected to be completed in July of 2006 and will reside on existing property at the Portland Mill.&#160; </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In 2004, the Company announced the permanent closure of the Napa Mill.&#160; In December 2005, the Company sold the Napa real estate which consisted of approximately 152 acres in Napa, California.&#160;&#160; The Company also recorded an impairment charge for the carrying value of the pipe mill equipment that will not be used at its other operating units.&#160;&#160;&#160; </font></p>

<p><font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Camrose Pipe Mill is located on approximately 67 acres in Camrose, Alberta, Canada, with the large diameter line pipe mill and the ERW pipe mill occupying approximately four acres and three acres, respectively.&#160; In addition, there is a 3,600 square foot office building on the site.&#160; The sales staff leases office space in Calgary, Alberta, Canada.&#160; The property, plant and equipment of the Camrose Pipe Mill, and certain other assets, are collateral for the Camrose (CDN) $15 million revolving credit facility (see Note 7 to the Company&#146;s Consolidated Financial Statements, &#147;<i>Debt, Financing Arrangements and Liquidity</i>&#148;).</font></p>
<p  align="center">
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">12</font></p>

<div style="page-break-before:always"></div>
<PAGE>
<br>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In 2005, the Company purchased the real estate occupied by its Columbia Structural Tubing operation.&#160; The real estate was formerly occupied under a sublease by the Company.&#160; The real estate consists of 25 acres of land in the Rivergate Industrial Park in Portland, Oregon and a 175,000 square foot manufacturing/warehouse structure.&#160; The structure houses leased equipment consisting of a slitting line, a structural tubing mill and a proprietary in-line coating system. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In 2004, the Company entered into a 10-year loan agreement to purchase a 50% interest in a warehouse.&#160; The warehouse resides near the Portland Mill.&#160; Both the Portland Mill and CST use a portion of the warehouse for storage.&#160; The warehouse resides on approximately 25 acres in the Rivergate Industrial Park and includes total warehouse area of approximately 234,000 square feet and office area of approximately 11,600 square feet.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b><i>RMSM Division</i></b></font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Pueblo
Mill is located in Pueblo, Colorado on approximately 570 acres.&#160; The
operating facilities principally consist of an electric arc furnace, a ladle
refining furnace and vacuum degassing system, a 6-strand continuous round caster
for producing semi-finished steel, and three finishing mills (a rail mill, a
seamless pipe mill, and a rod and bar mill). Operations at the seamless pipe
mill were suspended from November 2003 until December 2005.&#160; In December
2005, the Company reopened the seamless mill, with shipments beginning in
January 2006.</font></p>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company is a party to various other claims, disputes, legal actions and other proceedings involving contracts, employment, and various other matters. In the opinion of management, the outcome of these matters should not have a material adverse effect on the consolidated financial condition of the Company.</font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company maintains insurance against various risks, including certain types of tort liability arising from the sale of its products.&#160; The Company does not maintain insurance against liability arising out of waste disposal or on-site remediation of environmental contamination because of the high cost of that coverage.&#160; In addition, the Company&#146;s per claim deductible for workers&#146; compensation claims is $2 million due to the high cost of maintaining that insurance with a lower deductible.&#160; There is no assurance that the insurance coverage carried by the Company will be available in the future at reasonable rates, if at all.</font></p>

  <p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman"><b>MARKET FOR REGISTRANT&#146;S COMMON EQUITY, RELATED STOCKHOLDER MATTERS   AND ISSUER PURCHASES OF EQUITY SECURITIES</b></font></p>  </td>

<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company&#146;s common stock is traded on the New York Stock Exchange.&#160; At February 17, 2006, the number of common stockholders of record was 822.&#160; See Part II, Item 8, &#147;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data &#150; Quarterly Financial Data,&#148; for information on quarterly dividends and common stock prices. </font></p>
<p>
<font size="2" face="Times New Roman">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Indenture under which the Company&#146;s 10% Notes were issued contains potential restrictions on new indebtedness and various types of disbursements, including common stock dividends.&#160; One of the restrictions on cash dividends is based on the cumulative amount of the Company&#146;s consolidated net income, as defined.&#160; The Company has not paid dividends in recent history, and at this time does not intend to pay dividends in 2006.</font></p>
